THA approaches and complications.md:
## 1. Indications and pre-operative planning
- **Indications:** end-stage hip arthritis (primary OA, inflammatory arthritis, AVN, post-traumatic, DDH, Perthes/SCFE sequelae), **displaced femoral neck fractures in active elderly**, failed fixation, tumours.
- **Contraindications:** active infection (joint or systemic), neuropathic (Charcot) joint (relative), severe abductor deficiency (relative: use constrained/dual mobility), medically unfit.
- **Templating** (calibrated AP pelvis, magnification about 20%): **restore the centre of rotation, femoral offset and leg length**; cup at the **teardrop** (medial border) and inferior at the teardrop line; femoral component size and neck cut level; **offset** (reduced offset weakens the abductors and increases impingement/dislocation; excessive offset causes trochanteric pain).
- **Leg length:** measured to the **inter-teardrop line** from the lesser trochanters; **lengthening over about 2-4 cm** risks **sciatic nerve palsy** (peroneal division).

## 2. Surgical approaches
| Approach | Interval / technique | Advantages | Risks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Posterior (Southern/Moore, Kocher-Langenbeck)** | Split gluteus maximus; release **short external rotators (piriformis, gemelli, obturator internus) and posterior capsule** | **Commonest**, extensile, preserves abductors, good femoral exposure | **Higher dislocation (posterior)** (reduced by **capsule and rotator repair**, about 1% with repair vs 4% without), **sciatic nerve** injury |
| **Direct lateral (Hardinge, transgluteal)** | **Split gluteus medius** (anterior third to half) and vastus lateralis (no true internervous plane) | **Low dislocation**, good exposure | **Superior gluteal nerve** injury if the split goes **over about 5 cm above the greater trochanter tip** (abductor weakness, **Trendelenburg gait/limp**), heterotopic ossification |
| **Anterolateral (Watson-Jones)** | Between **tensor fasciae latae and gluteus medius** (both superior gluteal nerve: not a true internervous plane) | Low dislocation | Superior gluteal nerve (inferior branch to TFL), abductor damage |
| **Direct anterior (Smith-Petersen/Hueter)** | **Superficial: sartorius (femoral) and TFL (superior gluteal)**; **deep: rectus femoris (femoral) and gluteus medius (superior gluteal)**: true internervous plane | Muscle-sparing, **low dislocation**, supine position (fluoroscopy, leg length), possibly faster early recovery | **Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (meralgia paraesthetica; up to 15-80% transient numbness)**, **femoral fractures** (calcar, greater trochanter) during broaching, wound problems in obese patients, learning curve, **ascending branch of LFCA** (ligate) |
| Trochanteric osteotomy (Charnley) | Greater trochanter osteotomised | Wide exposure (complex primaries, revision) | **Trochanteric non-union/escape**, wire problems |

- **Long-term outcomes are similar** between approaches; choose by surgeon experience and patient factors.
- **Femoral neurovascular structures** lie anterior: anterior retractors placed too medially over the anterior acetabular rim can injure the **femoral nerve/artery**.

## 3. Acetabular component position
- **Lewinnek "safe zone":** **inclination (abduction) 40 ±10 degrees**, **anteversion 15 ±10 degrees** (radiographic). Many dislocations occur within this zone, so the **functional (spinopelvic) position** matters: a **stiff lumbar spine** (fusion, degenerative) changes the safe zone (adjust anteversion, consider dual mobility).
- **Combined anteversion (cup + stem) about 25-45 degrees** (Ranawat test/Dorr).
- **Wallace/Hip-spine:** see spinopelvic notes.
- **Steep inclination (over 50 degrees)** = edge loading, increased wear, **squeaking (ceramic-on-ceramic)**, metal ion release (metal-on-metal), dislocation. **Excessive anteversion** = anterior dislocation; **retroversion** = posterior dislocation.
- **Acetabular screws (Wasielewski quadrant system):** a line from the ASIS through the centre of the acetabulum, and a perpendicular: **posterosuperior quadrant = safe** (screws up to about 25 mm+; sciatic nerve and superior gluteal vessels if too long), **posteroinferior = relatively safe** (sciatic, inferior gluteal, internal pudendal), **anterosuperior = "death zone" (external iliac artery and vein)**, **anteroinferior = obturator nerve and vessels**.

## 4. Fixation
- **Cemented femoral stems:** **taper-slip (polished, collarless: Exeter, CPT)** subside within the cement mantle creating radial compressive forces (excellent long-term survival), or **composite-beam (shape-closed, matt, collared: Charnley)** bonded to cement. **Third-generation cementing:** **pulsatile lavage, distal cement restrictor/plug, vacuum mixing (reduces porosity), retrograde filling with a gun, pressurisation, stem centralisers**, mantle **2 mm or more** (avoid thin mantle/defects: Barrack grading A-D).
- **Uncemented stems:** fixation by **bone ingrowth (porous coating, pore size 50-400 microns)** or **ongrowth (grit-blasted)**; **hydroxyapatite coating** enhances osseointegration; **micromotion under about 40-150 microns** required. **Stress shielding:** proximal bone loss with **stiff, large, extensively coated stems** (Engh); proximal femoral bone loss (Gruen zones 1 and 7).
- **Cups:** mostly uncemented (press-fit, **under-reaming 1-2 mm**, ± screws); cemented polyethylene cups in elderly/poor bone.
- **Age-related trends:** cemented stems reduce **periprosthetic fracture** risk in the elderly (registries: **uncemented stems have higher early periprosthetic fracture rates over about 75 years**).
- **Gruen zones (femur):** 7 zones on AP (1 greater trochanter, 4 tip, 7 calcar), 14 including lateral; **DeLee-Charnley zones (acetabulum)** I-III.

## 5. Complications
### Dislocation
- **About 1-3% after primary THA**; the commonest cause of early revision in some registries.
- **Risk factors:** **posterior approach without repair**, **component malposition**, **small head size** (**larger heads (32-36 mm) increase jump distance and impingement-free arc**), **reduced offset/soft tissue tension**, abductor deficiency, **neuromuscular disease, cognitive impairment, alcohol**, **spinal fusion/stiffness**, **revision surgery**, female sex, **previous hip surgery**, **fracture as indication**.
- **Early dislocations** (within 3 months) with well-positioned components: **closed reduction** and precautions/brace (about 2/3 do not recur). **Recurrent or malpositioned:** revise: reposition components, **dual-mobility** cup, **larger head**, **constrained liner** (last resort, higher failure), **trochanteric advancement**, abductor reconstruction.
- **Dual-mobility bearings:** small head within a large mobile polyethylene liner inside a polished shell: large effective head, very low dislocation; **intraprosthetic dislocation** is a unique complication.

### Periprosthetic fracture (Vancouver classification, femur)
| Type | Location | Stem | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A_G / A_L** | Greater / lesser trochanter | Stable | Non-operative unless displaced (A_G: fix if displaced over 2.5 cm/abductor function) |
| **B1** | Around/just below the stem | **Stable (well-fixed)** | **ORIF** (locking plate + cables, ± strut allografts) |
| **B2** | Around the stem | **Loose**, good bone stock | **Revision with a long stem** (distal fixation, e.g. tapered fluted modular) bypassing the fracture by 2 cortical diameters |
| **B3** | Around the stem | **Loose, poor bone stock** | **Revision with proximal femoral replacement** (elderly) or allograft-prosthesis composite (young) |
| **C** | Well below the stem tip | Stable | **ORIF** (overlap the stem to avoid stress risers) |

- **Distinguishing B1 from B2 is critical**: **a significant proportion of "B1" are actually loose**: test stability intraoperatively; look for radiolucent lines, subsidence, cement mantle fracture.
- **Intraoperative fractures:** commoner with **uncemented press-fit stems**; calcar cracks: **cerclage cable**.
- **Unified Classification System (UCS)** applies to all periprosthetic fractures (see paediatric/trauma notes for type definitions: A apophyseal, B bed of implant (B1 stable, B2 loose, B3 poor bone), C clear of implant, D dividing two implants, E each of two bones, F facing an implant).
- **Acetabular periprosthetic fractures (Paprosky).**

### Leg-length discrepancy
- Commonest cause of litigation; lengthening under 1 cm usually tolerated. **True LLD** (bony) vs **apparent/functional** (pelvic obliquity, contractures). **Sciatic palsy risk with lengthening over about 2.5-4 cm.**

### Nerve injury (about 0.5-3%)
- **Sciatic nerve (peroneal division)** commonest (posterior approach, lengthening, DDH/revision, retractor placement, cement); **femoral nerve** (anterior retractors), **superior gluteal nerve** (lateral approach), **lateral femoral cutaneous** (anterior approach), obturator (screws/cement).

### Heterotopic ossification (HO)
- **Brooker classification:** **I** bone islands in soft tissue; **II** spurs with **over 1 cm** between opposing surfaces; **III** under 1 cm gap; **IV** apparent **bony ankylosis**.
- **Risk factors:** **ankylosing spondylitis, DISH, previous HO**, hypertrophic OA, Paget disease, **male sex**, **lateral/transtrochanteric approaches**, head injury.
- **Prophylaxis** (high-risk patients): **NSAIDs (indomethacin for about 6 weeks)** or **single-dose radiotherapy (about 7-8 Gy) within 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery**. Excision of mature HO (normal alkaline phosphatase, bone scan quiescent, usually after 6-12 months) with prophylaxis.

### Venous thromboembolism
- **DVT without prophylaxis up to about 40-60%**; fatal PE about 0.1-0.5%. **Prophylaxis: LMWH, rivaroxaban/apixaban/dabigatran (DOACs), or aspirin** (**CRISTAL trial** (2022): aspirin had more symptomatic VTE than enoxaparin after arthroplasty; **PEPPER trial**: aspirin, warfarin, rivaroxaban compared), plus **mechanical prophylaxis and early mobilisation**. Extended prophylaxis about **28-35 days after THA** (about 10-14 days after TKA).

### Others
- **Infection (about 1%)**, see PJI notes. **Aseptic loosening** and **osteolysis** (wear particles: see bearing notes), **trunnionosis/taper corrosion** (head-neck junction; metal ions; ALTR), **squeaking** (CoC), **iliopsoas impingement** (cup prominent anteriorly; groin pain on resisted hip flexion; **iliopsoas tenotomy or cup revision**), **greater trochanteric pain syndrome**, **vascular injury**, **bone cement implantation syndrome** (hypotension, hypoxia, cardiac arrest during cementing, especially elderly with fractures), **medical complications**.

## 6. Special situations
- **DDH (Crowe classification by proximal migration of the head):** **I under 50%**, **II 50-75%**, **III 75-100%**, **IV over 100%** subluxation (relative to femoral head height). **Hartofilakidis** (dysplasia, low dislocation, high dislocation). Place the **cup at the true acetabulum** (anatomical centre), small cups, structural autograft/medialisation, **subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy** (Crowe IV) to prevent sciatic stretch; femur often **narrow and excessively anteverted** (modular or cemented stems to control version).
- **Protrusio acetabuli** (rheumatoid arthritis, Paget, Marfan, osteomalacia): **medial wall bone grafting**, lateralise the centre of rotation, cages/rings in severe cases.
- **Paget disease:** bleeding (consider pre-op bisphosphonates), deformity (osteotomy), hard sclerotic bone, HO.
- **Sickle cell, post-fixation, post-acetabular fracture, ankylosed hip** (abductor function uncertain), **neuromuscular hips**, **young patients** (bearing choice).

> Exam pearl: **Posterior approach = commonest, higher dislocation without capsular repair; Hardinge = superior gluteal nerve 5 cm above the trochanter (Trendelenburg); direct anterior = lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and femoral fractures.**

> Exam pearl: **Lewinnek: inclination 40 ±10, anteversion 15 ±10. Anterosuperior acetabular quadrant = external iliac vessels (death zone); posterosuperior = safe.** Larger heads and dual mobility reduce dislocation.

> Exam pearl: **Vancouver B1 stable = ORIF; B2 loose = long-stem revision; B3 loose + poor bone = proximal femoral replacement/APC; C = ORIF.** **Brooker HO I-IV; prevent with indomethacin or radiotherapy (7-8 Gy) in high-risk patients.**

TKA balancing and alignment.md:
## 1. Alignment concepts
- **Mechanical axis of the lower limb:** centre of the femoral head to the centre of the ankle; normally passes **just medial to the centre of the knee** (about 0-3 degrees varus overall).
- **Anatomical vs mechanical femoral axis:** differ by about **5-7 degrees (valgus)**; the **distal femoral cut is made at about 5-7 degrees valgus to the anatomical axis** (perpendicular to the mechanical axis).
- **Joint line:** the native tibial plateau is in **about 3 degrees varus** relative to the tibial mechanical axis; the distal femur in about 3 degrees valgus relative to the femoral mechanical axis; the **joint line is roughly parallel to the floor in stance** (with feet together).
- **Alignment philosophies:**

| Philosophy | Principle | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanical alignment (MA)** | Femoral and tibial cuts **perpendicular to their mechanical axes** (neutral HKA, joint line horizontal); balance by **soft-tissue releases** | Traditional gold standard; **neutral axis ±3 degrees** associated with better survival (debated with modern implants) |
| **Anatomical alignment** (Hungerford) | Joint line at 3 degrees varus, neutral limb | Historical |
| **Kinematic alignment (KA)** | **Resurface the pre-arthritic joint** (restore native joint lines and HKA), **minimal releases** | Implants positioned within the patient's native alignment; outlier limb alignments; satisfaction similar or slightly better in some trials |
| **Restricted KA / inverse kinematic / functional alignment** | KA within safe limits; robotic gap-based adjustments | **CPAK classification** (Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee: arithmetic HKA and joint line obliquity; 9 phenotypes) describes constitutional alignment |

- **Robotic/navigation** TKA reduces alignment outliers; clinical superiority not yet proven.

## 2. Bone cuts and component rotation
- **Tibial cut:** perpendicular to the tibial mechanical axis in the coronal plane (MA), **posterior slope about 3-7 degrees** (CR knees more; PS knees less, as excess slope can cause instability in flexion/post impingement). Resect about **8-10 mm from the unaffected (higher) side** (measured resection).
- **Distal femoral cut:** about 5-7 degrees valgus to the anatomical axis (intramedullary guide entry point just medial and anterior to the PCL origin); resection equal to the implant thickness (about 9-10 mm).
- **Femoral component rotation (critical for patellar tracking and flexion gap balance):**
  - **Transepicondylar axis (TEA)** (lateral epicondyle to the **medial epicondylar sulcus**: surgical TEA): **most reliable** rotational landmark.
  - **Whiteside line (AP axis):** from the deepest part of the trochlear groove to the centre of the intercondylar notch; femoral component **perpendicular** to it (unreliable in trochlear dysplasia).
  - **Posterior condylar axis (PCA):** femoral component **externally rotated about 3 degrees** relative to it (because the medial posterior condyle is larger); **beware a hypoplastic lateral condyle in valgus knees** (would internally rotate the component: use TEA/Whiteside).
  - **Gap balancing technique:** rotate the femoral component so the **flexion gap is rectangular** after the tibial cut with balanced ligaments.
- **Tibial component rotation:** aligned to the **medial third of the tibial tubercle** (Akagi line: PCL attachment to the medial border of the patellar tendon at its tibial attachment).
- **Internal rotation of femoral or tibial components** (combined) causes **patellar maltracking, lateral subluxation, anterior knee pain, patellar complications and stiffness** (Berger: combined internal rotation 1-4 degrees = tilt; 3-8 = subluxation; 7-17 = dislocation/failure). Assess with **CT**.
- **Anterior femoral notching** (anterior cortex): increases **supracondylar periprosthetic fracture** risk (about 30-40% reduction in torsional strength).
- **Femoral sizing:** **anterior referencing** (cuts the posterior condyles by the measured amount; downsizing changes the flexion gap: may loosen flexion) vs **posterior referencing** (restores posterior condylar offset; risk of anterior notching or overstuffing the patellofemoral joint).

## 3. Gap balancing
- **Extension gap** (distal femoral cut + tibial cut) and **flexion gap** (posterior femoral cut + tibial cut) must be **equal and rectangular**.
- **The tibial cut affects both gaps; the distal femoral cut affects only the extension gap; the posterior femoral cuts/femoral size affect only the flexion gap.**

| Problem | Flexion gap | Extension gap | Solution |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tight in both** | Tight | Tight | **Cut more tibia** |
| **Loose in both** | Loose | Loose | **Thicker polyethylene insert** (or augments) |
| **Tight in extension, OK in flexion** | Balanced | Tight | **Release posterior capsule / remove posterior osteophytes**, then **resect more distal femur** (about 2 mm) |
| **Loose in extension, OK in flexion** | Balanced | Loose | **Distal femoral augmentation** (add distal femur), thicker insert + smaller/posterior cut (combined) |
| **Tight in flexion, OK in extension** | Tight | Balanced | **Downsize the femoral component** (anterior referencing) or **increase tibial slope**; release PCL (CR) |
| **Loose in flexion, OK in extension** | Loose | Balanced | **Upsize femur** (posterior augments) or **thicker insert + more distal femoral resection** |

- **Joint line:** keep within about **8 mm** of native: **elevation of the joint line** (excess distal femoral resection + thick insert) causes **mid-flexion instability, patella baja (pseudo), patellofemoral problems**.

## 4. Coronal deformity correction (soft-tissue releases)
### Varus knee (commonest)
- **Tight medial structures:** remove **medial osteophytes first** (tibial and femoral), then release **deep MCL (meniscotibial)**, **posteromedial capsule/semimembranosus** (tight in **extension**), **superficial MCL** (subperiosteal from tibia or **pie-crusting**; the **anterior sMCL is tight in flexion**, posterior in extension), **pes anserinus** (rarely). **PCL** release (in CR knees with tight flexion).
- Also: **medial tibial reduction osteotomy** (downsize/lateralise the tibial tray and remove medial bone).
- **Fixed flexion deformity:** remove posterior osteophytes, **posterior capsular release**, gastrocnemius recession; as a last resort extra distal femoral resection.

### Valgus knee
- **Tight lateral structures:** **iliotibial band** (tight in **extension**), **popliteus** (tight in **flexion**), **lateral collateral ligament** (tight in **flexion and extension**), **posterolateral capsule** (extension), lateral head of gastrocnemius, biceps femoris.
- **Order (Ranawat inside-out pie-crusting, Whiteside):** posterolateral capsule, ITB, then popliteus/LCL as needed.
- **Hypoplastic lateral femoral condyle**: do not use the PCA alone for rotation.
- **Peroneal nerve palsy** risk when correcting **severe valgus with flexion contracture** (stretch): **flex the knee post-operatively**, loosen dressings; explore if no recovery.
- **Ranawat valgus types:** I (correctable, medial soft tissue intact), II (fixed, medial attenuated: may need constraint), III (severe osseous deformity with incompetent medial structures: constrained implant).

## 5. Constraint and design choices
| Design | Mechanism | Indications |
|---|---|---|
| **Cruciate-retaining (CR)** | PCL retained; flatter or ultra-congruent inserts | Intact, functional PCL; less bone resection; **paradoxical anterior femoral sliding** |
| **Posterior-stabilised (PS)** | **Cam-post** substitutes the PCL (**femoral rollback**) | **Absent/incompetent PCL**, **patellectomy**, inflammatory arthritis, large deformity, previous HTO (debated); risks: **post wear/fracture, patellar clunk syndrome** (fibrous nodule at the superior pole catching the box), cam jump (flexion instability) |
| **Medial pivot / ultra-congruent** | Highly conforming medial compartment | Mimics native kinematics |
| **Varus-valgus constrained (CCK, non-linked)** | Tall, wide post in a deep box | **MCL/LCL incompetence**, severe valgus, flexion-extension mismatch, revisions |
| **Rotating-hinge (linked)** | Hinged femur-tibia linkage with rotation | **Global ligamentous deficiency**, severe bone loss, distal femoral replacement (tumour/fracture), hyperextension instability, **neuromuscular recurvatum** (polio) |

- **Use the least constraint needed** (more constraint = more stress transfer to fixation interfaces = loosening).
- **Mobile-bearing vs fixed-bearing**: no proven difference in survival; spinout risk with mobile bearings.
- **Patellar resurfacing:** reduces **reoperation for anterior knee pain** (meta-analyses, KAT trial: little functional difference); inflammatory arthritis favours resurfacing. **Patellar thickness should be restored** (avoid overstuffing). **Patellar complications:** maltracking (component internal rotation, lateral placement of femoral/tibial components, medial placement of patellar button is preferred), **fracture** (over-resection, avascular after lateral release), **avascular necrosis**, **patellar clunk**, loosening, tendon rupture.
- **Patellar tracking:** **"no thumb" test**; lateral retinacular release if needed (protect the **superior lateral genicular artery**).

## 6. Complications of TKA (non-infective)
- **Stiffness/arthrofibrosis** (flexion under about 90 degrees at 6-12 weeks): **manipulation under anaesthesia (within about 6-12 weeks)**, arthrolysis, revision.
- **Instability:** **flexion instability** (flexion gap larger than extension; recurrent effusions, PS cam jump), **mid-flexion instability**, **genu recurvatum**, global instability: revise with balanced gaps/increased constraint.
- **Aseptic loosening/osteolysis**, **polyethylene wear**.
- **Periprosthetic fractures:** **supracondylar femur (Lewis-Rorabeck I undisplaced, II displaced + stable prosthesis (ORIF: locking plate or retrograde nail if open box), III loose prosthesis (revision/DFR))**; **tibial (Felix)**; **patella (Goldberg/Ortiguera)**.
- **Peroneal nerve palsy** (valgus, flexion contracture, epidural anaesthesia), **vascular injury** (popliteal artery behind the posterior capsule: **posterolateral corner, about 9 mm from the posterior tibia in flexion**).
- **Wound complications:** **use the most lateral previous incision** (lateral skin flap less perfused: blood supply from the medial side), skin bridges at least about 5-6 cm.
- **Extensor mechanism disruption:** patellar tendon rupture (**worst; augment with allograft or synthetic mesh, medial gastrocnemius flap**), quadriceps rupture.
- **VTE**, **persistent pain** (about 10-20% dissatisfied after TKA: highest predictors are pre-operative expectations, pain catastrophising, mild radiographic OA).
- **Unexplained painful TKA** work-up: **exclude infection first (ESR/CRP, aspiration)**, then instability, malrotation (CT), loosening, patellar issues, referred pain (hip, spine), CRPS, neuroma.

> Exam pearl: **Tibial cut affects both gaps; distal femoral cut affects extension only; posterior femoral cut/femoral size affects flexion only. Tight both = cut more tibia; loose both = thicker insert.**

> Exam pearl: **Femoral rotation: TEA most reliable; 3 degrees external to the posterior condylar axis; Whiteside line perpendicular. Internal rotation of components = patellar maltracking. Tibial rotation: medial third of the tubercle.**

> Exam pearl: **Varus: medial osteophytes, deep MCL, posteromedial capsule/semimembranosus, then superficial MCL. Valgus: ITB (extension), popliteus (flexion), LCL (both); peroneal palsy risk with valgus + flexion contracture.** Least constraint necessary; rotating hinge for global ligament loss.

bearing surfaces and wear.md:
## 1. Tribology basics
- **Wear:** removal of material from articulating surfaces. **Mechanisms:**
  - **Adhesive** (commonest in metal-on-polyethylene: polymer transfers to the counterface and is pulled off),
  - **Abrasive** (hard asperities or particles plough the softer surface),
  - **Third-body** (trapped particles: cement, bone, metal debris),
  - **Fatigue/delamination** (subsurface cracking; important in **TKA**, low-conformity, oxidised polyethylene),
  - **Corrosive** (fretting at modular junctions).
- **Modes of wear (McKellop):** **Mode 1** intended bearing surfaces; **Mode 2** a primary surface against a non-intended secondary surface (e.g. head against shell after liner wear-through); **Mode 3** third-body particles between primary surfaces; **Mode 4** two non-intended surfaces rubbing (back-side wear of a liner against the shell, neck against the cup rim, **trunnion corrosion**).
- **Lubrication:** **fluid-film** (ideal; surfaces fully separated: ceramic-on-ceramic and well-designed metal-on-metal with large heads and low clearance), **boundary** (surfaces in contact, lubricant adsorbed: metal-on-polyethylene), **mixed**. Lambda ratio (fluid-film thickness / combined surface roughness) **over 3 = full fluid-film**.
- **Linear wear** (penetration of the head into the liner, mm/year) vs **volumetric wear** (mm³/year: **determines particle load and osteolysis**). **Volumetric wear increases with head size** (V = π r² w, Charnley); **linear wear decreases with larger heads**.
- **Osteolysis threshold** for conventional polyethylene: **about 0.1 mm/year linear wear** (Dumbleton); above this, osteolysis is common.

## 2. Biology of particle disease (osteolysis)
- **Wear particles (0.1-1 micron polyethylene most bioactive)** are phagocytosed by **macrophages**, which release **TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, PGE2**, upregulate **RANKL** on osteoblasts/stromal cells: **osteoclast activation** and bone resorption. The **effective joint space** (Schmalzried) lets particles migrate along the implant-bone interface.
- **Clinical:** often **silent** until large lesions, loosening or fracture; **serial radiographs**, **CT** for extent (pelvic lesions underestimated on radiographs).
- **Treatment:** **liner exchange and bone grafting** of lytic lesions with retained well-fixed components (risk of dislocation after isolated liner exchange: use larger heads), or full revision for loose components.

## 3. Polyethylene
- **UHMWPE (ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene):** semi-crystalline polymer. **Gamma irradiation** (sterilisation) breaks chains forming **free radicals**: in air, these **oxidise** (embrittlement, **subsurface white band**, delamination, worse with **shelf ageing**).
- **Sterilisation:** gamma in **inert gas/vacuum** packaging, **ethylene oxide** or **gas plasma** (no cross-linking, no free radicals).
- **Highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE):** irradiated at **5-10 Mrad** to cross-link chains (**much lower adhesive/abrasive wear**: **wear reduced about 80-90%**, dramatic fall in osteolysis and revision for wear in THA); **post-irradiation thermal treatment** removes free radicals: **remelting (above the melting point, about 137 C: eliminates free radicals but reduces crystallinity, fatigue strength and fracture toughness)** or **annealing (below melting: preserves mechanical properties but leaves some free radicals: in-vivo oxidation)**. **Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol)-infused/blended HXLPE** quenches free radicals without remelting.
- **Cross-linking reduces fatigue strength and toughness**: concern in **TKA (high contact stress, fatigue wear)** and thin liners, **rim/locking mechanism fractures** with thin liners and large heads or malposition.
- **Polyethylene thickness:** **at least 6-8 mm** in TKA (thinner = high contact stress, delamination).
- **Compression-moulded (direct)** polyethylene has better wear performance than **ram-extruded + machined** stock in TKA; **Hylamer** (failed); **calcium stearate**-free resins.
- **TKA wear:** fatigue-dominated (**delamination, pitting**) because of **low conformity**, rolling/sliding, high contact stresses; **backside wear** of modular inserts (micromotion against the tray) contributes to tibial osteolysis.

## 4. Metal-on-polyethylene (MoP)
- **Cobalt-chromium or ceramic heads on HXLPE**: the commonest and most proven bearing in THA (excellent long-term registry survival).
- **Head size:** **32-36 mm** heads with HXLPE balance dislocation risk and wear; very thin liners for large heads risk fracture.

## 5. Ceramics
- **Alumina (Al2O3)** and **zirconia-toughened alumina (BIOLOX delta, ZTA)**: **hardest, most scratch-resistant, very low wear, inert particles, excellent wettability (hydrophilic: fluid-film lubrication)**, **lowest wear of all bearings (ceramic-on-ceramic)**.
- **Problems:** **brittleness** (fracture: much rarer with delta ceramics, about 0.002-0.02%), **squeaking** (about 1-3%: associated with **cup malposition (edge loading)**, **stripe wear**, impingement), **chipping on insertion** (malseating), **limited neck lengths**, cost.
- **Ceramic head fracture:** revise to a **ceramic head** (not metal: **third-body ceramic particles** cause catastrophic metal head wear) with full synovectomy; use a new taper sleeve if the trunnion is damaged.
- **Ceramic-on-polyethylene:** reduces polyethylene wear vs metal heads (smoother, harder, more wettable), avoids taper corrosion (trunnionosis) of CoCr heads.
- **Oxidised zirconium (Oxinium):** zirconium alloy with a **ceramic oxide surface layer**: low wear against polyethylene with metal toughness; **avoid against a damaged surface**: if the thin layer is breached (e.g. after dislocation and closed reduction over the cup rim), the soft substrate wears rapidly.
- **Old zirconia (yttria-stabilised) heads** suffered **phase transformation** (Prozyr recall 2001).

## 6. Metal-on-metal (MoM)
- **Cobalt-chromium on cobalt-chromium**; large heads possible (hip resurfacing: **Birmingham Hip Resurfacing**; large-head THA). Low volumetric wear in ideal conditions but **nanometre-sized metal particles** (huge numbers) and **metal ions (cobalt, chromium)**.
- **Adverse reactions to metal debris (ARMD) / adverse local tissue reaction (ALTR):** **pseudotumours** (solid or cystic masses), **ALVAL** (aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis-associated lesion: type IV delayed hypersensitivity), **metallosis**, **soft-tissue necrosis** (abductor destruction). **Systemic cobalt toxicity:** cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, hypothyroidism, visual/hearing loss.
- **Risk factors:** **female sex**, **small component size**, **steep cup inclination (over about 50-55 degrees: edge loading)**, **specific designs (ASR recall 2010)**, large-head MoM THA (trunnion corrosion), bilateral implants, renal impairment.
- **Surveillance (MHRA/FDA):** **blood cobalt and chromium levels** (concern **over about 7 µg/L (ppb)**; some use 2-4 µg/L for unilateral resurfacing as threshold for closer monitoring), **MARS MRI** (metal artefact reduction sequence) or ultrasound for pseudotumours.
- **Revision** for symptomatic patients, rising ions, enlarging pseudotumours or osteolysis; revise to a **ceramic or polyethylene** bearing. **Outcomes of revision for ALTR are worse** than for other aseptic causes.
- **Hip resurfacing:** **young, active men with large femoral heads** (best results; **avoid in women, small heads, osteoporosis, large cysts, AVN, DDH**). **Femoral neck fracture** (commonest early failure; **notching** of the neck, varus positioning).
- **Metal hypersensitivity** in TKA (nickel) is debated (rarely a true cause of failure; diagnosis of exclusion).

## 7. Taper corrosion (trunnionosis)
- **Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion** at the **head-neck (and modular neck-stem) junction**: micromotion disrupts the passive oxide layer: fretting + crevice corrosion: **cobalt release**, **ALTR even with metal-on-polyethylene**.
- **Risk factors:** **large CoCr heads** (larger moment arm/torque), **long necks/high offset**, **dissimilar metals (CoCr head on titanium stem)**, small/short trunnions, **dual-taper modular necks** (recalled designs), poor taper assembly (blood/fluid on the taper, inadequate impaction).
- **Diagnosis:** **raised cobalt >> chromium** (Co:Cr ratio over about 3-5 suggests taper corrosion rather than bearing wear), **MARS MRI**.
- **Treatment:** **revise the head to a ceramic head with a titanium sleeve**, change liner, debride; revise the stem if the trunnion is badly damaged.

## 8. Choosing a bearing (summary)
| Bearing | Wear | Particles | Main concerns | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **MoP (CoCr on HXLPE)** | Low (with HXLPE) | Polyethylene (osteolysis) | Taper corrosion with large CoCr heads | **Most patients** |
| **Ceramic-on-HXLPE** | Lower | Polyethylene | Cost; ceramic fracture (rare) | Younger/active patients; avoid taper issues |
| **Ceramic-on-ceramic** | **Lowest** | Ceramic (inert) | **Squeaking, fracture, chipping**, cup position sensitive | Young active patients |
| **MoM** | Low (volumetric) but ions | **Metal nanoparticles/ions** | **ALTR/pseudotumour, systemic cobalt** | Largely abandoned except selected resurfacing |

- **Hardness (decreasing):** ceramic > CoCr > stainless steel > titanium > polyethylene. **Titanium is never used as a bearing surface** (poor wear resistance, notch sensitivity).
- **Wettability (hydrophilicity):** ceramics best.

> Exam pearl: **Volumetric wear determines osteolysis; larger heads = more volumetric, less linear wear (with conventional PE). Osteolysis threshold about 0.1 mm/year. Particles of 0.1-1 micron activate macrophages, TNF-alpha, RANKL.**

> Exam pearl: **HXLPE reduces THA wear about 80-90%; remelting removes free radicals but lowers fatigue strength; annealing keeps strength but leaves free radicals; vitamin E is the alternative.** TKA wear is fatigue/delamination (conformity and thickness at least 6-8 mm).

> Exam pearl: **Ceramic-on-ceramic: lowest wear; squeaking and fracture; revise a broken ceramic head with a new ceramic head. MoM: pseudotumour/ALVAL, women, small sizes, steep cups; check cobalt/chromium and MARS MRI. Trunnionosis: cobalt much higher than chromium.**

periprosthetic infection (ICM criteria).md:
## 1. Epidemiology and pathogenesis
- **Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI)** occurs in about **1-2% of primary hip and knee arthroplasties** (higher in revisions, about 3-5%). Among the commonest causes of revision (leading cause of early TKA revision).
- **Biofilm:** bacteria adhere to the implant, produce an **extracellular polymeric matrix (glycocalyx)**; sessile bacteria are **up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics** and protected from host defences. **Biofilm matures within about 3-4 weeks**: the basis for implant retention only in early infections.
- **"Race for the surface"** (Gristina): host cells vs bacteria competing to colonise the implant.
- **Organisms:** **coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis) and S. aureus** (together about 50-60%), streptococci, enterococci, gram-negatives, anaerobes; **Cutibacterium acnes** (shoulder, low-grade), fungi (Candida); **polymicrobial** (about 10-15%); **culture-negative** (about 7-15%: prior antibiotics, fastidious organisms).
- **Routes:** perioperative contamination (most), **haematogenous** (late acute; dental, urinary, skin, endocarditis), contiguous spread.

## 2. Risk factors
- **Patient:** **diabetes (HbA1c over about 7.5-8%, perioperative glucose over about 200 mg/dl)**, **obesity (BMI over 40)**, **smoking**, **malnutrition (albumin under 3.5 g/dl, transferrin under 200, lymphocytes under 1,500)**, **rheumatoid arthritis/immunosuppression**, **S. aureus colonisation (nasal carriers)**, chronic kidney/liver disease, **prior joint surgery/infection**, **intra-articular steroid injection within about 3 months**, IV drug use, anaemia, male sex, depression.
- **Surgical:** prolonged operative time, **allogeneic transfusion**, haematoma, persistent wound drainage (over about 5-7 days), revision surgery, concurrent infection elsewhere.

## 3. Prevention
- **Optimise** glucose, BMI, nutrition, smoking cessation (4-6 weeks), treat dental/urinary infection.
- **MRSA/MSSA screening and decolonisation** (**nasal mupirocin + chlorhexidine body washes**).
- **Prophylactic antibiotics:** **cefazolin within 60 minutes before incision** (vancomycin within 120 minutes if MRSA-colonised or beta-lactam allergic; clindamycin alternative); **redose** after about 4 hours or with large blood loss (over 1,500 ml); **stop within 24 hours**. Antibiotic-loaded cement in high-risk patients.
- **Skin preparation:** **chlorhexidine-alcohol** (superior to povidone-iodine in surgical site infection trials), hair clipping (not shaving) just before surgery.
- **Theatre:** **laminar flow**, restricted traffic, **dilute povidone-iodine lavage** before closure (debated benefit), meticulous haemostasis, tranexamic acid (fewer transfusions).

## 4. Classification by timing (management-oriented)
| Type | Timing | Features | Typical organism |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Early post-operative (acute)** | **Within about 4 weeks (up to 3 months in some systems)** of surgery | Wound drainage, erythema, fever, pain | S. aureus, gram-negatives |
| **Acute haematogenous** | Any time, **symptoms under about 3 weeks** in a previously well-functioning joint | Sudden pain, effusion, sepsis | S. aureus, streptococci |
| **Chronic (late)** | **Over about 4 weeks**/insidious | Persistent pain, early loosening, sinus tract | CoNS, C. acnes |
| Positive intraoperative cultures | Unexpected positive cultures at revision for "aseptic" failure | **Two or more positive**: treat as PJI (about 6 weeks) | CoNS, C. acnes |

- **Tsukayama classification:** I positive intraoperative cultures, II early post-operative, III acute haematogenous, IV late chronic.

## 5. Diagnosis
### Clinical
- **Pain** (commonest symptom), stiffness, effusion, wound problems, **sinus tract** (pathognomonic), fever (often absent in chronic infection), **early loosening** (within 5 years).

### 2018 ICM (International Consensus Meeting / Parvizi) definition
- **Major criteria (either = infected):**
  1. **Two positive cultures of the same organism** (by standard culture methods).
  2. **A sinus tract communicating with the joint or visualisation of the prosthesis.**
- **Minor criteria (pre-operative scoring):**

| Criterion | Score |
|---|---|
| **Serum CRP over 1 mg/dL (10 mg/L)** or **D-dimer over 860 ng/mL** | **2** |
| **Serum ESR over 30 mm/h** | **1** |
| **Synovial WBC over 3,000 cells/µL** or **positive leukocyte esterase (++)** | **3** |
| **Positive alpha-defensin** (signal-to-cutoff ratio over 1) | **3** |
| **Synovial PMN over 80%** | **2** |
| **Synovial CRP over 6.9 mg/L** | **1** |

  - **Total 6 or more = infected; 2-5 = possibly infected** (add intraoperative findings); **0-1 = not infected**.
- **Intraoperative findings** (for inconclusive pre-operative scores): **positive histology (over 5 neutrophils per high-power field in 5 or more fields: 3 points)**, **purulence (3 points)**, **single positive culture (2 points)**; combined score **6 or more = infected**, 4-5 inconclusive, 3 or less not infected.
- **Thresholds differ for the early post-operative period** (within 6 weeks): **CRP over 100 mg/L (knee/hip acute)**, synovial WBC over about **10,000**, PMN over about **90%** (inflammation from surgery raises markers).
- **Inflammatory arthritis, crystal disease, metallosis (ALTR)** can give false-positive synovial counts (manual count in metallosis).
- **EBJIS 2021 definition** (European Bone and Joint Infection Society) uses "infection likely/confirmed" tiers with similar markers.

### Practical work-up (AAOS/ICM)
1. **Serum ESR and CRP** in every painful arthroplasty (high sensitivity: if both normal, PJI unlikely).
2. If raised (or high suspicion): **joint aspiration** (stop antibiotics at least **2 weeks** before aspiration) for **synovial WBC, PMN%, culture** (aerobic + anaerobic; **hold cultures 10-14 days** if C. acnes or low-virulence organisms suspected), **leukocyte esterase**, **alpha-defensin**.
3. **Intraoperative:** **5 (3-6) separate tissue samples** with separate instruments, **frozen section**, **sonication** of explants (improves culture yield, especially after antibiotics), avoid swabs.
4. **Imaging:** radiographs (early loosening, periosteal reaction, osteolysis); nuclear imaging (labelled leukocyte with marrow scan) when aspiration is inconclusive; MRI with MARS sequences.

## 6. Treatment
### Debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR)
- **Indications:** **early post-operative (within about 4 weeks)** or **acute haematogenous (symptoms under 3 weeks)** infection, **well-fixed implants**, **healthy soft tissue (no sinus)**, susceptible organism.
- **Technique:** radical **synovectomy and debridement**, high-volume lavage (dilute povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine), **exchange of all modular parts** (head and liner/polyethylene insert: essential), followed by **pathogen-specific antibiotics** (**rifampicin** added for staphylococci with retained implants: active against biofilm; never as monotherapy; **fluoroquinolones for gram-negatives**) for about **3 months (hip) to 6 months (knee)**.
- **Success about 50-80%**; worse with **S. aureus/MRSA**, delays, high CRP, rheumatoid arthritis, prior DAIR. **Repeated DAIR** has poor results. **KLIC and CRIME80 scores** predict DAIR failure.

### One-stage exchange
- Remove all components, radical debridement, re-implant new components (often **antibiotic-loaded cement**), specific antibiotics. Increasingly used for **chronic infection** with **known organism and susceptibilities**, healthy soft tissues, no sinus (debated), immunocompetent host (Frankfurt/ENDO-Klinik practice). Similar control rates to two-stage in selected cases, fewer operations.

### Two-stage exchange (traditional gold standard for chronic PJI, especially in North America)
1. **Stage 1:** remove all components and cement, radical debridement, **antibiotic-loaded cement spacer** (static or **articulating**; high-dose antibiotics: e.g. **vancomycin + gentamicin/tobramycin**; heat-stable antibiotics, about **3-4 g of antibiotic per 40 g cement**), followed by **4-6 weeks of IV/oral antibiotics**.
2. **Antibiotic holiday** (about 2 weeks; debated) and assessment of infection control (**ESR/CRP trends, aspiration**: no single test reliably confirms eradication).
3. **Stage 2:** re-implantation (often after **6-12 weeks**), intraoperative cultures/frozen section.
- **Success about 85-90%**. **Interim mortality and failure to reach stage 2** are significant in elderly patients.
- **After re-implantation:** a further **3 months of oral antibiotics** reduced failure in one RCT (Frank et al.).

### Salvage
- **Resection arthroplasty (Girdlestone for the hip)**, **knee arthrodesis** (intramedullary nail or external fixation), **amputation** (uncontrolled infection, life-threatening sepsis, massive bone/soft-tissue loss), **long-term suppressive antibiotics** (unfit patients or retained infected implants).

### Antibiotic principles
- Bactericidal, biofilm-active agents with good bone penetration: **rifampicin (staphylococci)**, **fluoroquinolones (gram-negatives)**; adjust to cultures; **monitor toxicity** (rifampicin interactions, vancomycin nephrotoxicity, linezolid myelosuppression).
- **Oral vs IV:** **OVIVA trial** (2019): **oral antibiotics were non-inferior to IV** within the first 6 weeks for bone and joint infection (including PJI), with fewer line complications.
- **Duration:** **DATIPO trial** (2021): **12 weeks of antibiotics** was superior to 6 weeks for PJI (DAIR/one-stage/two-stage) in persistent infection rates.

## 7. Special situations
- **Acute haematogenous infection with a well-fixed implant:** DAIR quickly (ideally within days of symptom onset).
- **Fungal PJI:** two-stage, antifungal-loaded spacer (amphotericin/voriconazole), prolonged antifungals; poor outcomes.
- **C. acnes** (shoulder): slow growing (hold cultures 14 days), male, young, previous shoulder surgery.
- **Antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures** in arthroplasty patients: **not routinely recommended** (AAOS/ADA), except selected immunocompromised patients.

> Exam pearl: **2018 ICM major criteria: two positive cultures of the same organism, or a sinus tract. Minor: CRP/D-dimer (2), ESR (1), synovial WBC over 3,000 or LE ++ (3), alpha-defensin (3), PMN over 80% (2), synovial CRP (1); 6 or more = infected.**

> Exam pearl: **DAIR (with modular exchange) for early post-operative (within 4 weeks) or acute haematogenous infection (under 3 weeks symptoms) with stable implants; add rifampicin for staphylococci. Chronic infection: one- or two-stage exchange.** OVIVA: oral non-inferior; DATIPO: 12 weeks beats 6.

> Exam pearl: **Biofilm matures in about 3-4 weeks; CoNS and S. aureus are commonest; stop antibiotics 2 weeks before aspiration; take 5 tissue samples; sonicate implants.** Cefazolin within 60 minutes of incision; chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep.

revision arthroplasty.md:
## 1. Why arthroplasties fail
- **THA (registries):** **aseptic loosening/osteolysis** (commonest long-term), **dislocation/instability**, **infection**, **periprosthetic fracture**, adverse reaction to metal debris, leg-length/pain.
- **TKA:** **infection** (commonest cause of early revision), **aseptic loosening** (commonest long-term), **instability**, **arthrofibrosis**, polyethylene wear (historical), periprosthetic fracture, malalignment/malrotation, extensor mechanism failure, unexplained pain.
- **Time-dependence:** **early (under 2 years)**: infection, instability, malposition, fracture; **late**: wear, osteolysis, loosening.
- **Golden rule:** **every painful or failing arthroplasty is infected until proved otherwise**: **ESR/CRP ± aspiration** before any revision.

## 2. Evaluation before revision
- History (pain pattern: start-up thigh pain suggests femoral stem loosening; groin/buttock pain suggests acetabular loosening), wound history, systemic symptoms.
- **Infection work-up** (ICM criteria).
- **Serial radiographs:** **radiolucent lines over 2 mm, progressive**, **subsidence**, **component migration**, cement fracture, **pedestal formation** (distal endosteal bone around an uncemented stem tip: loose), **spot welds** (bone ingrowth: stable), osteolysis, polyethylene wear (eccentric head position).
  - **Engh criteria** for uncemented stem fixation (bony ingrowth vs fibrous stable vs unstable).
  - **Harris criteria** for cemented femoral loosening: **definite** (migration of the stem, cement fracture, stem fracture), **probable** (continuous radiolucent line around the entire cement mantle), **possible** (lucency over 50-100% of the interface).
- **CT** (osteolysis, component version, bone stock), **MARS MRI** (ALTR), **bone scan** (loosening is non-specific), **metal ions** (MoM, taper).
- **Implant identification**, operative notes, extraction tools, components and allograft availability, **neurovascular** proximity (intrapelvic cement/components: CT angiography).

## 3. Bone loss classifications
### Acetabulum: Paprosky
| Type | Rim | Columns | Migration / landmarks | Reconstruction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | Intact, minimal bone loss | Intact | No migration | **Hemispherical uncemented cup** |
| **II** (A, B, C) | Distorted (IIA superomedial, **IIB superolateral (rim deficient under 1/3)**, IIC medial wall) | **Intact (supportive)** | **Superior migration under 3 cm**; teardrop and ischium intact | **Hemispherical (jumbo) cup ± screws, particulate graft** |
| **IIIA** ("up and out") | Superolateral rim deficient (30-60% of circumference) | Partially supportive | **Over 3 cm superior migration**, **Kohler line intact**, moderate ischial and teardrop lysis | **Jumbo cup + porous metal augments (trabecular metal)** or structural allograft |
| **IIIB** ("up and in") | Over 60% rim loss | **Non-supportive** | **Kohler line breached**, severe ischial lysis, teardrop obliterated; **pelvic discontinuity** risk | **Cup-cage**, **custom triflange**, **augments + cage**, **distraction technique** |

- **Pelvic discontinuity:** separation of the superior and inferior hemipelvis through the acetabulum (**fracture line through both columns, medial translation/rotation of the inferior hemipelvis, broken Kohler line**). Treat with **posterior column plating + cup**, **cup-cage**, **acetabular distraction**, or **custom triflange**.
- **AAOS classification:** I segmental, II cavitary, III combined, IV pelvic discontinuity, V arthrodesis.

### Femur: Paprosky
| Type | Bone loss | Reconstruction |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | Minimal metaphyseal loss (like primary) | Primary-type stem (cemented or uncemented) |
| **II** | **Metaphyseal loss**, **intact diaphysis** | **Extensively porous-coated (cylindrical) stem** or **modular tapered stem** |
| **IIIA** | Metaphysis non-supportive, **over 4 cm of intact isthmus** for scratch fit | **Extensively porous-coated stem** (diaphyseal fixation) or **modular tapered fluted (Wagner-type)** |
| **IIIB** | **Under 4 cm** of intact isthmus | **Modular tapered fluted titanium stem** |
| **IV** | **Extensive diaphyseal loss, widened canal**, no isthmus support | **Impaction allografting (cemented, Exeter technique)**, **allograft-prosthesis composite (young)**, **proximal femoral replacement (elderly)** |

- **Extensively coated cylindrical cobalt-chromium stems** fail when the canal is **over about 18-19 mm** (stiff, stress shielding, less isthmus); **tapered fluted titanium stems** (modular or monoblock) are now widely used for most femoral revisions (reliable distal fixation, rotational stability via flutes).
- **Extended trochanteric osteotomy (ETO):** for **removing well-fixed stems/cement**, correcting proximal deformity (varus remodelling); length about **10-15 cm** (two-thirds of the trochanter with the lateral cortex); fix with cables; allows distal fixation **at least 4-6 cm below the osteotomy**.

### Knee: Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute (AORI)
| Type | Bone loss | Reconstruction |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Intact metaphysis**, small defects | **Cement ± screws**, standard components |
| **2A** | Damaged metaphysis, **one condyle/plateau** | **Augments (metal wedges/blocks)**, particulate graft |
| **2B** | Damaged metaphysis, **both condyles/plateaus** | Augments, **cones/sleeves** |
| **3** | **Deficient metaphysis**, often with collateral ligament/tendon detachment | **Metaphyseal cones (porous tantalum/titanium) or sleeves**, **structural allograft**, **hinged prosthesis**, **distal femoral/proximal tibial replacement** |

- **Three-zone fixation (Morgan-Jones):** **epiphysis (zone 1), metaphysis (zone 2), diaphysis (zone 3)**: aim for **solid fixation in at least two zones**; **metaphyseal fixation (cones/sleeves)** is key.
- **Stems:** **cemented** (shorter, fills canal) or **press-fit diaphyseal-engaging** (offset couplers to avoid tibial/femoral conflict).

## 4. Revision TKA principles
1. **Exposure:** medial parapatellar arthrotomy, synovectomy, release scar in the gutters, **external rotation of the tibia and medial release**; for difficult exposure: **quadriceps snip** (first choice; proximal oblique incision of the quadriceps tendon), **V-Y quadricepsplasty (turndown)** (extensor lag), **tibial tubercle osteotomy (TTO)** (long osteotomy, about 6-8 cm, fixed with wires/screws). **Avoid patellar tendon avulsion** (catastrophic): pin the tendon, use the snip/TTO early.
2. **Component removal:** preserve bone (osteotomes, saws, ultrasonic tools).
3. **Restore the tibial platform** first (establishes the joint line), then the **femur in flexion (size, rotation, posterior augments)**, then **extension**.
4. **Joint line restoration:** about **2.5 cm (one fingerbreadth) above the fibular head**, about **3 cm distal to the medial epicondyle**, **1 cm below the inferior pole of the patella**; avoid elevation (patella baja, mid-flexion instability).
5. **Constraint as needed** (PS, VVC, rotating hinge) to achieve stability with balanced gaps.
6. **Patella:** revise if loose/worn; patellar bone loss: **gull-wing osteotomy**, porous metal patellar augments, patelloplasty.

## 5. Revision THA principles
- **Approach:** usually posterior/extensile; **ETO** for stem/cement removal.
- **Acetabulum:** **uncemented hemispherical cups with screws** handle most defects (Paprosky I-IIIA), with **porous metal augments** for segmental loss; **impaction grafting with cemented cup** (Slooff) for contained defects; **cages/cup-cage/triflange** for IIIB/discontinuity.
- **Femur:** as per Paprosky; **cement-in-cement revision** (well-fixed intact cement mantle: re-cement a new taper-slip stem into the old mantle) for rapid revision with retained cement.
- **Instability prevention in revision:** **larger heads, dual-mobility cups** (reduce dislocation markedly in revision), **constrained liners** for abductor deficiency (high failure), **abductor reconstruction**.
- **Periprosthetic fracture revision** (Vancouver B2/B3) as in THA notes.

## 6. Complications of revision
- **Infection (higher than primary)**, **dislocation (up to about 10-15% in revision THA)**, **intraoperative fracture/perforation**, nerve injury, **aseptic re-loosening**, **extensor mechanism failure (TKA)**, wound breakdown (use previous lateral incision; **plastic surgery** input; medial gastrocnemius flap for exposed TKA), **thromboembolism**, **blood loss** (tranexamic acid, cell saver), **medical complications** (elderly).

## 7. Megaprostheses and salvage
- **Proximal femoral replacement (PFR)** / **distal femoral replacement (DFR)** / **total femur**: tumour resections, massive bone loss, elderly periprosthetic fractures (allows immediate weight bearing). **High dislocation (PFR)** and **infection rates (about 10%+)**; use **silver-coated** implants, mesh for soft-tissue attachment.
- **Allograft-prosthesis composite (APC):** younger patients (biological soft-tissue attachment).
- **Knee arthrodesis** (failed multiple revisions/infection with extensor loss), **above-knee amputation**, **resection arthroplasty** (Girdlestone hip).

> Exam pearl: **Every failing arthroplasty is infected until proved otherwise. TKA: infection = commonest early failure; THA long-term: aseptic loosening/osteolysis.**

> Exam pearl: **Paprosky acetabulum: II (rim/columns supportive, under 3 cm migration) = hemispherical cup; IIIA (up and out, Kohler intact) = jumbo cup + augments; IIIB (up and in, Kohler broken) = cup-cage/triflange; watch for pelvic discontinuity.**

> Exam pearl: **Paprosky femur: II/IIIA = extensively porous-coated or modular tapered; IIIB (under 4 cm isthmus) = modular tapered fluted; IV = impaction grafting/APC/PFR.** **AORI knee: 1 cement, 2 augments/cones, 3 cones/sleeves/hinge/replacement; fix in two of three zones.** **Revision TKA exposure: quadriceps snip first; protect the patellar tendon.**
